say.en: In 1896 Becquerel found that uranium salts fogged a wrapped photographic plate with no light at all. Some nuclei are unstable and, all on their own, throw out particles and energy to become other nuclei. In this lesson: Describe alpha, beta and gamma decay.
Write balanced decay equations.
Compare the properties of the three radiations.

body.en: In α *decay* a nucleus emits a helium-4 nucleus: $^{A}_{Z}X \to ^{A-4}_{Z-2}Y + ^{4}_{2}\text{He}$. In β⁻ decay a neutron becomes a proton: $^{A}_{Z}X \to ^{A}_{Z+1}Y + e^- + \bar\nu$; in β⁺ decay a proton becomes a neutron, giving $^{A}_{Z-1}Y + e^+ + \nu$. In γ decay an excited nucleus falls to a lower energy state and emits a high-energy photon; A and Z do not change. In every decay, charge and the number of nucleons are conserved.

points.en: β⁻: Z + 1; β⁺: Z − 1; A unchanged
γ: no change in A or Z

narration.en: In α decay a nucleus emits a helium-4 nucleus: $^{A}_{Z}X \to ^{A-4}_{Z-2}Y + ^{4}_{2}\text{He}$. In β⁻ decay a neutron becomes a proton: $^{A}_{Z}X \to ^{A}_{Z+1}Y + e^- + \bar\nu$; in β⁺ decay a proton becomes a neutron, giving $^{A}_{Z-1}Y + e^+ + \nu$. In γ decay an excited nucleus falls to a lower energy state and emits a high-energy photon; A and Z do not change. In every decay, charge and the number of nucleons are conserved.

say.en: In alpha decay a nucleus emits a helium-4 nucleus: to the power A Z X to to the power A minus 4 Z minus 2 Y plus to the power 4 2 He. In beta⁻ decay a neutron becomes a proton: to the power A Z X to to the power A Z plus 1 Y plus e^- plus bar nu; in beta⁺ decay a proton becomes a neutron, giving to the power A Z minus 1 Y plus e^ plus plus nu. In gamma decay an excited nucleus falls to a lower energy state and emits a high-energy photon; A and Z do not change. In every decay, charge and the number of nucleons are conserved. alpha: A minus 4, Z minus 2.
beta⁻: Z plus 1; beta⁺: Z minus 1; A unchanged.
gamma: no change in A or Z.

say.en: Each press is one decay. Alpha moves the nucleus two steps down in both protons and neutrons. Beta minus turns a neutron into a proton. Try to reach the green ring, lead-206.
Radium-226 emits an alpha particle. Top numbers add up, bottom numbers add up.
Carbon-14 is a beta minus emitter: the atomic number rises by one.
Gamma decay only lowers the energy of the nucleus: the star marks an excited state.
Balancing a decay equation.

body.en: α particles carry charge +2e, ionise strongly and are stopped by a sheet of paper or a few cm of air. β particles are fast electrons (or positrons), ionise less and are stopped by a few mm of aluminium. γ rays are photons: uncharged, weakly ionising and very penetrating, cut down only by thick lead or concrete. In a magnetic field α and β bend in opposite directions; γ goes straight.

points.en: Deflection: α and β opposite ways; γ none

alpha particles carry charge plus 2e, ionise strongly and are stopped by a sheet of paper or a few cm of air. beta particles are fast electrons or positrons, ionise less and are stopped by a few mm of aluminium. gamma rays are photons: uncharged, weakly ionising and very penetrating, cut down only by thick lead or concrete. In a magnetic field alpha and beta bend in opposite directions; gamma goes straight. Ionising power: alpha > beta > gamma.
Penetrating power: gamma > beta > alpha.
Deflection: alpha and beta opposite ways; gamma none.

problem.en: ²³²Th (Z = 90) ends as ²⁰⁸Pb (Z = 82). How many α and β⁻ particles are emitted?

steps.en: To reach 82, Z must rise by 4: 4 β⁻ decays.

narration.en: Let us solve this together. ²³²Th (Z = 90) ends as ²⁰⁸Pb (Z = 82). How many α and β⁻ particles are emitted?

say.en: Let us solve this together. to the power 232Th Z equals 90 ends as to the power 208Pb Z equals 82. How many alpha and beta⁻ particles are emitted?
A falls by 24: 24 over 4 equals 6 alpha decays.
6 alpha lower Z by 12, to 78.
To reach 82, Z must rise by 4: 4 beta⁻ decays.
So the answer is 6 alpha and 4 beta⁻.

body.en: For a chain, divide the drop in A by 4 to get the number of α decays (β changes nothing in A). Then the β⁻ count = 2 × (number of α) − (drop in Z).
